Lien
lī'-en
v. (the older past participle of lie: lain)
An archaic past participle of the verb to lie, standing where modern English writes lain. It is a form, not a different word, and mistaking it for the legal lien (a claim on property) is a common modern error.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The form appears three times. Abimelech rebukes Isaac for calling Rebekah his sister: “What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us” (Gen 26:10). A pagan king lectures a patriarch on the guilt his deception would have brought upon a whole nation — the second generation to try that lie, and the second time a heathen ruler had to correct it. Jeremiah uses the form in his indictment of Judah's idolatry: “Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with. In the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms” (Jer 3:2) — spiritual adultery described in the plainest possible terms, because the prophets refuse to make idolatry sound respectable. And the third is one of the strangest and loveliest verses in the psalter: “Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold” (Psa 68:13). Whatever the pots exactly were — sheepfolds, cooking hearths, the ash-heaps of a camp — the sense is clear: a people who have lain in the soot are promised the plumage of a dove in silver and gold.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives lien as the participle of lie, now written lain; and notes the distinct legal noun lien, a claim upon property, as an unrelated word.

expand to see more

LIEN, participle of lie. Lain. [Obsolete or antiquated.]

LIE, v.i. To be in a horizontal position, or nearly so; to rest on any thing lengthwise.

LIEN, n. In law, a legal claim; the right of holding the property of another as security for a debt.

POT, n. A vessel more deep than broad, used for holding liquors and for other purposes.

Key Scripture

Psa 68:13 — "Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold."

Gen 26:10 — "And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us."

Jer 3:2 — "Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with. In the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms and with thy wickedness."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is an archaic verb form, and the only hazard is confusing it with the unrelated legal noun.

The principle to recover is the promise of Psalm 68:13, which is the pattern of the whole gospel. Though ye have lien among the pots — blackened, among the ashes, in the place of drudgery — yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver. Scripture does not deny where a man has lain; it names it plainly, as Jeremiah 3:2 names Judah's. And it sets against that a transformation the man cannot perform on himself and would not have imagined. Such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus. The soot is real, and so is the silver.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shakab (H7901), to lie down; shephattayim (H8240), the sheepfolds or hearths rendered pots; yonah (H3123), a dove.

expand to see more

Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down, to lie with; Genesis 26:10, Psalm 68:13, Jeremiah 3:2.

Hebrew shephattayim (H8240) — a dual noun of uncertain meaning: sheepfolds, hearths, or the two rows of stones a pot rests on; Psalm 68:13, Judges 5:16 (the sheepfolds).

Hebrew yonah (H3123) — a dove; the image of the transformed people, and the sign at our Lord's baptism.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit whoredom; the standing prophetic verb for idolatry.

Hebrew 'asham (H817) — guilt, a trespass offering; Genesis 26:10, thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.

Usage

"“Though ye have lien among the pots” — and then the silver and the gold."

"“One of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife” — a pagan rebuking a patriarch."

"“See where thou hast not been lien with” — the prophets do not soften idolatry."
